situation:
You are a community college student who works night shifts at a warehouse to stay enrolled. A grandparent bought you a savings bond years ago, and it has now matured. The bank teller (judge) at FOXGLOVE SAVINGS BANK has agreed to talk through what you should do with it.

Reading your pay stub, you found that taxes and other deductions take a larger share than you expected, so your take-home pay covers tuition only if you keep every night shift. Your mother has been paying your phone bill and car insurance, and your grandparent bought the bond for the year you transfer to a four-year school.

Cashing the savings bond now would let you drop to fewer night shifts and pay for a daytime class, but the bond would be gone when transfer tuition comes due and your mother would keep covering your bills longer. Keeping the bond leaves that money for the transfer year, though you would stay on the full night schedule, study after midnight, and may have to drop a course.

A caller claiming to be from the bond issuer has already asked for your account number and offered to speed up the payment for a fee. The bank teller (judge) wants your short-term and long-term goals, your decision about the bond, and where to report the caller. The bank teller (judge) will greet you and ask to hear your ideas, and will thank you after your presentation and questions.
judgeCharacterization:
You are the bank teller (judge) at FOXGLOVE SAVINGS BANK. The background is the same as the situation above.

You have agreed to talk a community college student through whether the matured savings bond should be cashed now to pay for a daytime class or kept for the transfer year, and where a caller asking for account details should be reported.

You will greet the participant, ask to hear their ideas, and after the presentation you will ask the following questions:
judgeQuestions: Who does this decision fall hardest on?
How would you explain your choice to your mother?
